text: After this you can define the purpose, boundaries, fieldwork, and reporting plan for an energy audit.

Start an audit by agreeing on the decision it must inform. Define the sites, systems, intended depth, operating conditions, data requests, and expected report. A quick screening visit cannot support the same conclusions as detailed measurement. Plan access and instruments around qualified staff, site procedures, and safety restrictions; electrical enclosures must not be opened by unqualified people.

items: Agree the decision the owner needs. You should see: A written objective and scope. If not: Ask which investment or operational choice the audit must support.
Request past utility records, plans, and operating schedules. You should see: A checklist of received records. If not: Mark each unavailable record as a gap.
Select the visit team and measuring instruments. You should see: Named roles and an instrument plan. If not: Do not improvise access to restricted equipment.
Tour systems and interview operations staff. You should see: Observed equipment and schedule notes. If not: Record conflicting accounts separately.
Estimate opportunities and uncertainties. You should see: A list with evidence and assumptions. If not: Identify measurements needed before approval.
Issue findings and agree on follow-up. You should see: A report and responsible next actions. If not: Revisit claims that lack measured support.

Inferred: Illustrative case: A facilities manager needs an initial ranking for two sites. Collect the existing bills, agree on the walkthrough boundaries, and define report outputs. Hold back equipment-specific savings claims until actual usage is checked.

text: The audit proceeds from a question through evidence to a report and follow-up.
Pick audit depth from the decision risk.
A short inspection cannot prove an investment-grade result.
